title: Most Believe in Artificial Intelligence, but Many Do not Want to Try -- Providers' Attitude Towards Artificial Intelligence in India's Informal Healthcare Sector - A Case of TB Diagnosis (Preprint)
abstract: BACKGROUND Tuberculosis (TB) is a major global health concern, causing 1.5 million deaths in 2020. Diagnostic tests for TB are often inaccurate, expensive, and inaccessible, making chest X-rays (CXRs) augmented with Artificial Intelligence (AI) a promising solution. However, whether providers are willing to adopt AI is not apparent. OBJECTIVE The study seeks to understand the attitude of AYUSH (Ayurveda, Yoga and Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha, and Homoeopathy) and informal healthcare providers, who we jointly call AIPs, towards adopting AI for TB diagnosis. We chose to study these providers as they are the first point of contact for a majority of TB patients. METHODS We conducted a cross-sectional survey of 406 AIPs across the states of Jharkhand (162 participants) and Gujarat (244 participants) in India. We designed the survey questionnaire to assess the AIPs’ confidence in treating presumptive tuberculosis (TB) patients; their trust in local radiologists’ reading of the CXR images; their beliefs regarding the diagnostic capabilities of AI; and their willingness to adopt AI for TB diagnosis. RESULTS After removing incomplete responses, we found that 93.7% (270/288) of AIPs believed that AI improved the accuracy of TB diagnosis, and 69.4% (200/288) were willing to try AI. AIPs who were more confident in diagnosing TB and had greater trust in the local radiologists were more likely to believe in AI-based TB diagnosis. However, we found significant differences in AIPs’ willingness for AI adoption across the two states. Specifically, in Gujarat, a state with better and more accessible healthcare infrastructure, 73.4% (155/211) were willing to try AI; and in Jharkhand, 58.4.% (45/77) were willing to try AI. Moreover, AIPs in Gujarat who showed higher trust in the local radiologists were less likely to try AI. In contrast, in Jharkhand, those who showed higher trust in the local radiologists were more likely to try AI. CONCLUSIONS While most AIPs believed in the potential benefits of AI-based TB diagnosis, many did not intend to try AI, indicating that the expected benefits of AI measured in terms of technological superiority may not directly translate to impact on the ground. Improving beliefs among AIPs with poor access to radiology services or those who are less confident of diagnosing TB is likely to result in greater impact of AI on the ground.

summary.oneLiner: While most informal healthcare providers in India believe AI improves TB diagnosis, a significant gap remains between this belief and actual adoption intent.
summary.overview: This study examined how informal and traditional healthcare providers (AIPs) in India view using AI for tuberculosis (TB) diagnosis. Although nearly 94% of providers surveyed believe AI improves diagnostic accuracy, only about 69% expressed a willingness to use the technology. The findings reveal that geographic location and existing levels of trust in traditional local radiologists significantly influence whether a provider is open to adopting AI. Ultimately, the authors suggest that simply offering superior technology is not enough to ensure its use in frontline healthcare settings.
summary.question: What are the attitudes of AYUSH and informal healthcare providers towards adopting AI for TB diagnosis in India?
summary.method: A cross-sectional survey of 406 participants was conducted to assess confidence in TB treatment, trust in local radiologists, beliefs about AI capabilities, and willingness to adopt AI.
summary.data: The sample consists of 288 valid responses from AYUSH and informal healthcare providers across the states of Jharkhand and Gujarat, India.
findings: 93.7% of providers believed that AI improves the accuracy of TB diagnosis.
69.4% of providers expressed a willingness to try AI for TB diagnosis.
Providers who were more confident in diagnosing TB and had greater trust in local radiologists were more likely to believe in AI-based diagnosis.
Willingness to adopt AI varied by region, with 73.4% in Gujarat willing to try compared to 58.4% in Jharkhand.
In Gujarat, higher trust in local radiologists was associated with a lower likelihood of trying AI, whereas in Jharkhand, higher trust was associated with a greater likelihood of trying it.
summary.whyItMatters: The study suggests that technology developers and policymakers cannot assume that perceived technological superiority will lead to adoption. Efforts to promote AI should be tailored to specific local contexts, focusing particularly on providers who lack access to traditional radiology services or lack confidence in their own diagnostic capabilities.
